source.title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Optimization and Generalization for Overparameterized Two-Layer Neural Networks
source.authors: Sanjeev Arora; S. Du; Wei Hu; Zhiyuan Li; Ruo-Song Wang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own gradient-descent experiments on true, random, and partially corrupted labels, measuring convergence and generalization in two-layer ReLU networks. Its setup differs from the claim's standard stochastic-gradient settings.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports convergence comparisons for true, random, and worst-case labels; Figure 2 reports generalization measures across noise fractions. The paper also discusses Zhang et al. (2017), but those cited results are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes and experimentally compares fitting true and random labels using full-batch GD in two-layer ReLU networks. Its own results bear on V1 and the convergence comparison in V2, using a different training method from the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate: label projections onto kernel eigenvectors explain convergence differences, and the proposed complexity measure distinguishes true from random labels and tracks evaluation-error trends. It should specify that the corruption sweep randomizes both training and test labels.
record.recipe_differences: Two-layer ReLU network with fixed second-layer weights, only first-layer weights trained, full-batch GD, and small initialization scale; original claim concerns standard deep networks trained with stochastic gradient methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports faster convergence for true than random labels and plots generalization measures across random-label fractions; it also compares MNIST and CIFAR.

fits_no_version.finding: Generalization loss and classification error vary with label corruption when both training and test labels are randomized.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For matched corruption of training and evaluation labels, the proposed kernel complexity measure tracks the resulting evaluation-error trend.

record.problems: The empirical results are presented in figures without numeric values in the text. The experiments use only two classes from MNIST and CIFAR, a two-layer architecture with a fixed second layer, and full-batch GD; the study does not report chance-level test error for fully random labels.

untested.parts: Standard deep architectures trained with stochastic-gradient methods; an empirical numerical endpoint for random-label training error. Figure 2's chance-error endpoint uses randomized test labels.
A small constant-factor training-time overhead and convergence time across increasing corruption fractions are not established by the supplied text.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect empirical training fit throughout a corruption sweep together with steadily degrading test performance measured against unchanged true labels.
Comparisons involving weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or their removal.
Learning shared real patterns before memorizing noise within training on mixed labels. Separate true-label and random-label runs do not establish this temporal ordering.

missing.what: The study's own arbitrary-label trajectory result and explicit zero-training-error statement, distinguished from the convergence theorem attributed to Du et al. These supply fitting evidence absent from the extracted endpoint values.
missing.locator: Introduction, Our results; Sections 3.3 and 4, Theorems 3.2 and 4.1

record.verdict_notes: Missing numerical ratios, different architectures, and untested components are not themselves scope-limiting results. No V2 verdict is warranted from the qualitative speed ordering alone. The supplied text does not preserve readable plotted curves, so numerical endpoints or time ratios cannot be recovered.

versions.untested_parts: The reported experiments use two-layer ReLU networks with a fixed second layer and full-batch GD, not a range of standard deep networks or stochastic-gradient methods; exact training error and test error at chance for fully random labels are not numerically reported.

The paper reports qualitatively that true labels converge faster than random labels, but does not state a small constant-factor training-time comparison or report convergence time as corrupted-label fraction varies.

The experiments vary random-label fraction and plot generalization loss and classification error, but do not explicitly establish perfect training fit at every fraction or describe the error rise as steady.
